Vertex — Conversion Decline Investigation

iOS · Jan–Jul 2026
Summary 1. User mix 2. Region A decline 3. The build 4. Economy 4b. Resource spike 5. IAP Explorers
Executive Summary

First-time purchase conversion down ~40–47.8% since Feb — driven by a build, not traffic quality.

Two forces compound: user mix shifting away from Region A, and a real conversion drop within Region A starting the week build the build shipped.

Lead hypothesis: the build's FTUE changes (Fridge discounted 61.9%, progression condition loosened to accept any cheaper product) raised the barrier to a player's first purchase, while repeat purchasing held steady — a first-purchase acquisition problem, not general fatigue. A later economy change (post the build) compounded it by increasing resource held.

03

The build — the inflection point

A same-month, controlled comparison of app versions — and the full build-over-time trend.

Same-month conversion by version — March, May, June

Each colour = one calendar month, so within a colour, seasonality/geo/campaign mix are held constant. March shows the consecutive builds step. May and June confirm conversion never recovers to pre-the build levels even as later builds (the build, the build, the build) scale to full volume — it settles lower and keeps drifting down.

What shipped in the build (live 14 Mar 2026)

FTUE — Phase 1
Loosened early resource milestones: cashEarned_250 → 100, removed cashEarned_600 step. These were plausible first-purchase triggers.
FTUE Step 23
Changed Product-screen auto-open logic and progression gating.
FTUE Step 27
Fridge discounted 64.5% — removes the need to buy resource to afford it, directly undercutting a resource-purchase trigger point.
FTUE Step 24
Condition changed from orderedFruityBites to orderedProducts_3 — players can now progress by ordering any (often cheaper) product instead of the one that used to nudge a purchase.
A/B framework
Intrusive-ads & delivery-timing tests migrated Metica → Firebase.
Technical
Reworked IAP verification system — worth ruling out as a measurement artifact.

Conversion across every major build, with cohort size marked

Bars = install volume that month (right axis); line = conversion % (left axis). Conversion never recovers to the Feb (the build) baseline even as later builds (the build, the build, the build) scale to full volume.

Why we believe this is the primary cause

Decline is first-purchase-specific (repeat held steady, §5), version-specific (same-month step), and timed to the release. A pricing/seasonality story wouldn't produce all three at once.

04

The economy loosened after the build

A second, compounding driver: players holding more resource, reducing the need to buy.

After the build, median resource held increased — weakening the incentive for that first currency purchase, especially for resource/energy bundles. Compounding, not origin — decline predates the build by ~2 months.

04b

Digging into why resource balance spiked

Two independent cuts of the data — an A/B test and a plain weekend/weekday split — both point to the same thing: players are simply earning more resource, faster, in specific contexts. That's consistent with (and likely a contributor to) the economy loosening described above.

A. the Event: "Control" bucket holds meaningfully less resource than the 3 active-day variants

Comparing the 4 vipRushEvent variants against each other (users with no exposure to the test excluded), median resource balance for the Control bucket is lowest at 26 of 28 shop levels — and the gap widens as players progress, from roughly even at level 2–6 to a 15–17.6% gap by level 29. The same pattern holds for resource earned and spent (27/28 levels each), meaning Control players are less economically active in both directions, not just holding less.

Point A — read: at any given shop level, being in an active variant (Tue/Thu/Sat) of the the Event correlates with meaningfully higher resource earned, spent, and held than the Control/inactive bucket.

B. Independent of any A/B test: weekends show a sharp jump in resource earned/spent/balance from level 6 onward

Looking at the whole population (no test grouping at all), weekend resource earned is ~33.5% higher than weekday on average, spent ~30.3% higher, and balance ~20.6% higher. Critically, this effect is near-zero at shop levels 2–5 (the FTUE window) and switches on sharply at level 6, then holds steady for the rest of the game — consistent with longer weekend play sessions driving more economy throughput once players are past onboarding.

Resource earned — weekday vs weekend

Resource balance — weekday vs weekend

Because Saturday is one of the the Event's active-day variants, part of finding A may simply be riding this natural weekend effect rather than the event itself — worth isolating Tuesday/Thursday (weekday actives) from Saturday (weekend active) before crediting the event alone.

What this means for the resource-balance spike

Neither of these fully explains the build-level economy loosening from §4 on its own — both are relative comparisons (variant vs variant, weekend vs weekday) within the same time period, not a before/after view across builds. But they show the in-game economy is highly sensitive to session context (which day, which test bucket), which makes it very plausible that a small tuning change around the build (drop rates, event frequency, reward sizing) could produce a system-wide increase in resource held. Recommended next step: re-run the median-resource-by-build query (already written earlier) split by weekday vs weekend to confirm the the build jump holds after controlling for this day-of-week effect.

05

First-purchase decline on our biggest IAPs

The top 3 products drive ~55.7% of all first purchases. Their conversion is falling — and the two most front-loaded ones break exactly at the build.

First-time purchase conversion % — pick your own IAPs (monthly cohorts)

Weekly break — first purchase vs repeat, pick your own IAP

Offer A's first-purchase conversion breaks the week of 14 Mar; repeat conversion keeps rising through the same window. The change hurt acquisition of new payers, not willingness of existing ones.

First purchases are front-loaded to day 0

ProductDay 0By D1
Offer B is a day-0-or-never product (59.3% on day 0). Any disruption to the day-0 FTUE moment shows up almost instantly and completely — which is exactly the signature we see.

Blended conversion — first-time vs repeat, monthly

Blended conversion peaked in February (2.75%) and has declined every month since to 2.02% by June — a steady, real conversion decline rather than a one-off dip. This is the rate driving the absolute drop in new payers, since installs alone didn't fall nearly as much.

Finding: Offer A + Offer B drive ~46.6% of first purchases and both break the same week.
Finding: Offer A and Offer B drive ~42.8% of all first purchases and both break at the same week — the two most fragile pillars of the funnel. Switch to "Region A only" — the same March break shows up, unchanged, confirming it isn't a blended-country artifact.

F · Where each IAP's revenue comes from (by shop level)

Finding: Offer B/Offer A's early-level revenue share collapsed right at March.
Finding: Offer B and Offer A concentrate revenue in early levels (Offer B: ~8.9% of its own revenue from level 3 alone; Offer A peaks around levels 3-5) — both are effectively early-game products. The Manager Pass and Seasonal Pass lines are nearly flat across levels 12-28 with no single peak — they're bought steadily by longer-tenured players throughout the mid-late game, not tied to any one level.

Month-over-month, this early-game share collapsed right at March: Offer B's revenue from levels 1-3 fell from 26.5% (Jan) → 19.4% (Feb) → just 5.3% (Mar) → under 0.8% by April/May. Offer A shows the same break: 16.8% → 18.7% → 3.7% → under 0.8%. The early-game monetization moment for both products essentially disappeared the same month build the build shipped — direct product-level evidence for the FTUE-change hypothesis, not just a conversion-rate coincidence.
